When would you use cherry-pick?: Use `git cherry-pick` when you need to copy one or a few specific commits from another branch without merging the entire branch. A common example is applying an urgent production hotfix from `main` to a supported release branch: `git switch release/2.x && git cherry-pick <commit-sha>`. Git creates a new commit with the same change but a different SHA. Resolve any conflicts, run tests, and push through review. Avoid cherry-picking a long sequence of related commits because it duplicates history and makes future merges harder; in that situation, merge or rebase the complete branch instead.
What is git revert?: `git revert <commit-sha>` safely undoes a commit by creating a new commit containing the inverse change. It preserves the existing history, so it is the preferred way to undo a commit that has already been pushed to a shared branch. For example, `git revert a1b2c3d` opens a commit message and records the rollback; use `git revert -m 1 <merge-sha>` carefully for a merge commit. Resolve conflicts if necessary, run tests, and push the new revert commit. Unlike `git reset`, revert does not move the branch pointer or discard later commits.
What is git reset?: `git reset` moves the current branch pointer to another commit and optionally changes the staging area and working tree. `git reset --soft HEAD~1` moves HEAD but keeps changes staged; the default `git reset --mixed HEAD~1` keeps changes only in the working tree; `git reset --hard HEAD~1` discards tracked changes. Reset is useful for cleaning up local, unpublished history. Avoid resetting commits already pushed to a shared branch because pushing afterward usually requires a force push and can overwrite teammates' work. Use `git revert` for shared history.
What is the difference between reset and: `git reset` rewrites local branch history by moving the branch pointer; depending on `--soft`, `--mixed`, or `--hard`, it also changes the index and working tree. `git revert` preserves history and creates a new commit that reverses an earlier commit. Use reset for unpublished local mistakes, such as correcting the last commit before pushing: `git reset --soft HEAD~1`. Use revert for commits already shared on `main`: `git revert <sha>`. Reset may require a dangerous force push, while revert is auditable, collaborative, and normally safe to push.
What is a soft reset?: `git reset --soft <target>` moves HEAD and the current branch to the target commit but leaves both the staging area and working tree unchanged. The commits after the target disappear from the branch history, while all their changes remain staged for recommitting. For example, `git reset --soft HEAD~3` lets you combine the last three local commits into one using a new `git commit`. It is useful for reorganizing unpublished history without losing work. Do not use it casually on commits already pushed to a shared branch, because updating the remote would rewrite history.
What is a mixed reset?: A mixed reset moves HEAD and the branch pointer to the target commit, resets the staging area to match that commit, but preserves the files in the working tree. It is the default mode, so `git reset HEAD~1` equals `git reset --mixed HEAD~1`. The removed commit's changes become unstaged modifications, allowing you to edit them and selectively stage files again with `git add`. Use it to undo a local commit while keeping the code. As with other history-rewriting resets, avoid using it on shared, already-pushed commits.
What is a hard reset?: `git reset --hard <target>` moves HEAD and the branch pointer to the target commit, resets the staging area, and makes tracked working-tree files exactly match that commit. For example, `git reset --hard HEAD~1` removes the latest local commit and its tracked changes. Use it only when you intentionally want to discard local tracked work or restore a disposable branch. Check `git status`, save valuable work with a commit or stash, and confirm the target SHA first. Untracked files are not removed unless you separately run a command such as `git clean`.
Why is hard reset dangerous?: A hard reset is dangerous because it immediately discards tracked changes in both the staging area and working tree while moving the branch pointer. Unsaved edits can become difficult or impossible to recover, and resetting shared commits followed by `git push --force` can erase teammates' history. Before running it, inspect `git status` and `git log --oneline`, create a safety branch such as `git branch backup-before-reset`, or stash changes. If a local commit was removed, `git reflog` may help recover its SHA; uncommitted overwritten content may not be recoverable.
What is a redirect action in Cloud Armor: A redirect action in Google Cloud Armor tells the edge security policy to send matching traffic somewhere else instead of allowing it to reach the backend. It is commonly used with bot protection or WAF rules to redirect suspicious clients to a reCAPTCHA challenge or to return a configured redirect response. In a rule, you define the match expression, priority, and action, for example a Cloud Armor security policy rule that matches abusive paths or bot signals and uses redirect rather than deny. I would roll it out in preview first, check Cloud Armor logs for false positives, then enforce it only when legitimate users are not being redirected.
How do you apply a stash?: Use `git stash apply` to reapply the latest stash while keeping the stash entry, or `git stash apply stash@{n}` for a specific one. First run `git stash list`, confirm the target, then apply it from a clean working tree if possible. Resolve conflicts like a normal merge, run tests, and use `git status` to verify the result. Use `git stash pop` only when you want Git to remove the stash after a successful apply.
What is git reflog?: `git reflog` shows where HEAD and branch references have pointed recently, including commits that are no longer visible in normal branch history. It is local to your clone and is useful after mistakes like reset, rebase, checkout, or deleted branch recovery. Example: run `git reflog`, find the lost SHA, then recover with `git branch recovery <sha>` or `git reset --hard <sha>` if you are sure. Reflog is not a backup system forever; entries expire based on Git garbage-collection settings.
How can reflog recover a lost commit?: Run `git reflog` to find the SHA where your branch or HEAD pointed before the mistake, then create a safety branch from it: `git branch recovered-work <sha>`. After that, inspect with `git log recovered-work --oneline` and either merge, cherry-pick, or reset depending on the situation. For example, after an accidental `git reset --hard HEAD~1`, reflog normally still contains the removed commit. The safe pattern is branch first, inspect second, then change the main branch only after confirming the commit is correct.
What is an annotated tag?: An annotated tag is a full Git object that stores the tag name, target commit, tagger, date, message, and optionally a GPG signature. It is preferred for releases because it is auditable and can carry release notes. Create one with `git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "Release v1.2.0"` and push it using `git push origin v1.2.0`. In production workflows, annotated and signed tags help prove which commit was released. Avoid moving release tags after publishing unless your team has an explicit incident process.
What is a lightweight tag?: A lightweight tag is just a named pointer to a commit, similar to a branch that does not move. It has no tag message, tagger metadata, or signature. Create one with `git tag v1.2.0 <sha>`. It is fine for temporary local bookmarks, but I would avoid it for production releases because it carries less audit information. For release management, annotated tags are safer because they include metadata and can be signed. Verify tags with `git show v1.2.0` or `git rev-parse v1.2.0`.
How do you create a release tag?: First ensure the release commit is tested and merged, then create an annotated tag: `git switch main`, `git pull`, `git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "Release v1.2.0"`, and `git push origin v1.2.0`. Many pipelines trigger deployment from pushed tags, so tag only immutable release commits. If signing is required, use `git tag -s v1.2.0`. Validate with `git show v1.2.0` and confirm the CI/CD release job picked the same SHA. Avoid retagging published versions; create a patch version instead.
What is a detached HEAD state?: Detached HEAD means Git has checked out a commit directly instead of a branch, so new commits are not attached to a named branch. It often happens with `git checkout <sha>` or checking out a tag. It is safe for inspection or testing, but if you commit in this state, the work can become hard to find once you switch away. To keep it, create a branch: `git switch -c experiment-from-detached`. Use `git status` to confirm whether you are detached before making changes.
How do you recover from detached HEAD?: If you made commits in detached HEAD and want to keep them, create a branch before leaving: `git switch -c recovered-work`. If you already switched away, use `git reflog` to find the detached commit SHA and then run `git branch recovered-work <sha>`. After that, merge or cherry-pick the work into the correct branch. Do not panic and run random resets; first preserve the commit with a branch, then inspect it with `git log --oneline --decorate` and run tests.
What is squashing?: Squashing combines multiple commits into one commit, usually to make a feature branch easier to review and keep main history clean. A common command is `git rebase -i origin/main`, then mark follow-up commits as `squash` or `fixup`. Squashing is best for local or feature-branch cleanup before merge, not for rewriting shared main history. After squashing, run tests because conflict resolution or commit ordering can introduce mistakes. The trade-off is cleaner history versus losing some granular commit-by-commit debugging context.
Why should commits be squashed?: Squashing is useful when a branch has many noisy commits like `fix typo`, `try again`, or `address review`, and the final logical change is easier to understand as one commit. It improves review, release notes, revertability, and `git bisect` quality. For example, squash five work-in-progress commits into one clear commit before merging a small feature. Do not squash unrelated changes together, because rollback becomes harder. Also avoid rewriting a shared branch unless everyone agrees and force-push rules are understood.
What is interactive rebase?: Interactive rebase lets you edit a sequence of commits before they are shared or merged. Run `git rebase -i HEAD~5` to reorder, squash, fixup, edit messages, or drop commits. It is useful for cleaning feature-branch history before opening or merging a pull request. Because it rewrites commit SHAs, avoid using it on public/shared branches unless your team explicitly coordinates it. After resolving conflicts, continue with `git rebase --continue`, verify with `git log --oneline`, run tests, and push with `--force-with-lease` if needed.
How do you edit commit history?: For unpublished local history, use interactive rebase: `git rebase -i HEAD~n`. You can reword commit messages, squash commits, reorder them, edit a commit, or drop one. For the latest commit only, use `git commit --amend`. Because these operations rewrite SHAs, never casually rewrite shared history; use `git revert` for already-pushed commits on main. Before editing, check `git status`, create a backup branch, and after the rebase run tests and inspect `git log --oneline --graph`.
What is .gitignore?: `.gitignore` tells Git which untracked files or patterns should not be added to the repository. Typical entries include build output, logs, local environment files, dependency folders, and editor metadata, for example `node_modules/`, `.env`, `*.log`, or `dist/`. It does not remove files already tracked; for those, use `git rm --cached <file>` and commit the change. In production projects, `.gitignore` helps prevent secrets, generated artifacts, and machine-specific files from polluting the repository.
What should never be committed to Git?: Never commit secrets, private keys, cloud credentials, production `.env` files, tokens, certificates, customer data, large generated binaries, dependency directories, or machine-specific files. Examples include `service-account.json`, `.npmrc` with tokens, SSH keys, kubeconfigs, Terraform state files, and database dumps. Use secret managers, CI/CD credentials, `.gitignore`, pre-commit secret scanning, and protected branch checks. If a secret is committed, rotate it immediately; deleting the file in a later commit does not remove it from Git history.
What is Git LFS?: Git LFS stores large files outside normal Git object storage and keeps lightweight pointer files in the repository. It is useful for binaries such as datasets, models, videos, design assets, or archives that would make clone and fetch operations slow. Configure it with `git lfs install`, then track patterns like `git lfs track "*.psd"` or `git lfs track "*.bin"`. Commit the `.gitattributes` file so everyone uses the same rules. The trade-off is simpler large-file handling but dependence on LFS storage quotas and availability.
When is Git LFS required?: Use Git LFS when files are too large or change too often for normal Git history, such as ML model artifacts, datasets, media files, or packaged binaries. Normal Git stores every version forever, so large binary churn makes clones slow and repositories expensive. LFS keeps the repository lightweight by replacing content with pointer files and downloading real content on demand. Before adopting it, check platform quotas, CI support, backup policy, and whether an artifact registry, object storage bucket, or model registry is a better fit.
What are Git hooks?: Git hooks are scripts that run at specific Git lifecycle events such as before commit, before push, after merge, or on the server before accepting a push. Client hooks live under `.git/hooks`, while teams usually share managed hooks through tools like pre-commit because `.git/hooks` itself is not versioned. Common uses include formatting, linting, unit tests, commit-message checks, and secret scanning. Hooks improve feedback speed, but server-side CI and branch protection should still enforce critical controls because local hooks can be bypassed.
What is a pre-commit hook?: A pre-commit hook runs before Git creates a commit. It can block the commit if formatting, linting, tests, or secret scans fail. For example, using the `pre-commit` framework, teams define hooks in `.pre-commit-config.yaml` and developers run `pre-commit install`. This catches issues before code reaches CI. Keep hooks fast and deterministic; long integration tests belong in CI. Also remember pre-commit hooks are local controls, so important security and quality gates should be repeated in protected pipelines.
How can hooks enforce code quality?: Hooks enforce code quality by running automated checks at commit or push time, such as formatters, linters, type checks, unit tests, dependency checks, and secret scanning. A practical setup uses a versioned `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, installs hooks with `pre-commit install`, and mirrors the same checks in CI so bypassed local hooks are caught. Keep the local hook fast enough that developers do not disable it. For production teams, hooks are a first feedback layer; branch protection and CI remain the final enforcement layer.
How do you remove an accidentally commit: First rotate or revoke the secret immediately; assume it is compromised. Then remove it from the current code and history using a tool like `git filter-repo` or BFG, coordinate with the team, force-push the cleaned history, and ask everyone to reclone or carefully clean local copies. Also purge CI caches, artifacts, container images, and package registries that may contain the secret. Add prevention afterward: `.gitignore`, secret scanning, pre-commit hooks, protected CI checks, and moving credentials to a secret manager.
How do you prioritize incidents?: Incidents are prioritized by business and user impact, urgency, scope, and risk—not by which team reports them first. A complete production outage, security breach, or data-loss event is typically P1; severe degradation with a workaround is P2; limited-impact faults are P3 or P4. The priority is reassessed as evidence changes. A P1 immediately triggers an incident commander, paging, stakeholder communication, mitigation, and frequent updates. Restoration takes precedence over root-cause analysis; the detailed investigation follows after service is stable.
Can you explain your current/last GCP pr: My project was a [APPLICATION TYPE] platform running on GCP for [USERS/TRAFFIC SCALE]. Its architecture used [GKE/COMPUTE ENGINE/CLOUD RUN], [DATABASE], [NETWORKING COMPONENTS], and [CI/CD TOOL]. I owned [YOUR RESPONSIBILITIES], including deployments, Terraform changes, monitoring, incident response, security reviews, and cost optimization. Day to day, I reviewed alerts and SLOs, handled change requests, improved pipelines, troubleshot production issues, and coordinated releases with [TEAMS]. One measurable result was [VERIFIABLE RESULT], achieved by [SPECIFIC ACTION YOU PERSONALLY TOOK].
A Kubernetes Job runs one or more Pods until a finite task completes successfully. The Job controller retries failed Pods according to `backoffLimit` and considers the Job complete when the required completions succeed. Jobs suit database migrations, batch processing, and one-time maintenance; scheduled work uses a CronJob. Important fields include `completions`, `parallelism`, `activeDeadlineSeconds`, and `ttlSecondsAfterFinished`. Containers should be idempotent because retries can repeat work, and production Jobs need resource limits, observable exit codes, and cleanup policies.
A Kubernetes Secret stores sensitive configuration such as passwords, tokens, or TLS material and exposes it to Pods as environment variables or mounted files. Values in a manifest's `data` field are base64-encoded, not encrypted by themselves. Production clusters should enable encryption at rest, restrict access with RBAC, avoid committing Secret manifests to Git, and preferably integrate an external secret manager through CSI or an operator. Secret rotation must update consumers safely; applications mounting Secret volumes receive eventual file updates, while environment variables require Pod replacement.
A sidecar is a supporting container that runs beside the main application container in the same Pod, sharing its network namespace and optionally volumes. Common examples are log shippers, service-mesh proxies, and configuration reloaders. Kubernetes also supports native sidecars as restartable init containers by setting `restartPolicy: Always` in `initContainers`, which provides defined startup and shutdown ordering. Sidecars increase resource usage and operational coupling, so requests, limits, health behavior, security context, and failure impact must be designed independently from the main container.
Difference between ClusterIP and NodePor: ClusterIP exposes a Service on a virtual IP reachable only inside the cluster; it is the default and is used for internal service-to-service traffic. NodePort also creates a ClusterIP but additionally opens the same port, normally in the 30000–32767 range, on every node, making the Service reachable at `<node-ip>:<nodePort>`. NodePort is useful as a building block or for limited testing, but production external access usually uses a LoadBalancer, Ingress, or Gateway because they provide better routing, TLS, health checking, and exposure control.
Difference between LoadBalancer and Ingr: A Service of type LoadBalancer exposes one Kubernetes Service through an external or internal load balancer, commonly giving it a dedicated frontend IP. Ingress defines HTTP/HTTPS host- and path-based routing to multiple Services through one entry point, but it requires an Ingress controller to implement the rules. Use LoadBalancer for direct L4 exposure, including non-HTTP protocols; use Ingress for shared L7 routing and TLS termination. Gateway API is the newer, more expressive alternative for many HTTP and multi-team routing designs.
Workload Identity lets a Kubernetes workload obtain cloud permissions using its Kubernetes identity instead of a long-lived service-account key. In GKE, Workload Identity Federation for GKE maps a Kubernetes ServiceAccount principal to IAM authorization, either directly or through IAM service-account impersonation. The Pod receives short-lived credentials from the metadata service. Production configuration should bind only the required namespace and ServiceAccount, grant least-privilege IAM roles, disable key files, and verify both Kubernetes RBAC and Google Cloud IAM when troubleshooting authorization failures.
Pod affinity influences scheduling by requiring or preferring a Pod to run near other Pods matching specified labels. Rules use a label selector and a `topologyKey`, such as `kubernetes.io/hostname` for the same node or a zone label for the same availability zone. `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` is mandatory; if no node satisfies it, the Pod remains Pending. `preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` adds weighted preferences without blocking scheduling. Affinity can reduce latency, but excessive co-location harms failure isolation and can make scheduling slow or impossible.
A resource request is the CPU or memory amount Kubernetes uses for scheduling and, for CPU, relative runtime weighting. A limit is the maximum a container may consume. Exceeding a CPU limit causes throttling; exceeding a memory limit can trigger an OOM kill. If requests are too low, nodes become overcommitted and unstable; if too high, Pods remain Pending and capacity is wasted. Set values from observed usage and load tests, monitor throttling and OOM events, and use LimitRange or policy controls to prevent unbounded workloads.
A readiness probe determines whether a container is ready to receive traffic. When it fails, Kubernetes removes the Pod's endpoint from matching Services but does not restart the container. HTTP, TCP, gRPC, or exec probes can be used. The check should represent the application's ability to serve requests without depending on every optional downstream service, otherwise a shared dependency failure can remove all replicas. Configure `periodSeconds`, `timeoutSeconds`, and failure thresholds from real startup and transient-failure behavior, and use a startup probe for slow initialization.
A liveness probe detects a container that is running but cannot recover without a restart, such as a deadlock. After the configured failure threshold, kubelet restarts the container according to the Pod's restart policy. It supports HTTP, TCP, gRPC, and exec checks. A liveness probe must test an internal failure the process can fix by restarting; checking a shared database can create a restart storm during a database outage. Keep it lightweight, allow sufficient timeout and initial delay, and use a startup probe for slow-starting applications.
A startup probe determines whether an application has finished initializing. While it is failing, Kubernetes disables readiness and liveness evaluation, preventing slow-starting containers from being killed prematurely. Once it succeeds, Kubernetes stops running the startup probe and begins the normal probes. Its maximum startup allowance is approximately `failureThreshold × periodSeconds`. Use it for applications with long or variable initialization, but do not make the threshold unlimited: a genuinely stuck startup must eventually fail, surface events, and restart according to policy.
A PersistentVolumeClaim is a namespaced request for storage. It specifies requirements such as capacity, access mode, storage class, and optionally volume mode; Kubernetes binds it to a compatible PersistentVolume or dynamically provisions one through the selected StorageClass. Pods mount the claim rather than referencing the underlying disk directly. A Pending PVC usually indicates no matching PV, provisioning failure, topology constraints, quota, or CSI problems. Deletion behavior depends on the PV reclaim policy, so backup and retention requirements must be set before production data is stored.
A PersistentVolume is a cluster-scoped Kubernetes resource representing storage provisioned manually or dynamically through a CSI driver. It has capacity, access modes, volume mode, reclaim policy, and storage-specific connection details. A PVC binds to a compatible PV, and Pods consume the storage through that claim. `Retain` preserves the underlying asset after claim deletion; `Delete` normally removes dynamically provisioned storage. PV availability is not a backup strategy—production state still needs snapshots, tested restores, encryption, and topology-aware scheduling.
A StorageClass defines how Kubernetes dynamically provisions persistent storage. It identifies the CSI provisioner and parameters such as disk type, encryption, replication, filesystem, and binding behavior. `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer` delays provisioning until a Pod is scheduled, allowing the volume to be created in the correct zone. `reclaimPolicy` controls whether storage is deleted or retained after claim deletion, and `allowVolumeExpansion` permits supported PVC growth. Separate classes should express real service levels rather than exposing every provider option to application teams.
The HorizontalPodAutoscaler changes a workload's replica count from observed metrics such as CPU, memory, or custom/external metrics. For CPU utilization, it compares current utilization against the target relative to configured requests and calculates a desired replica count, then applies stabilization and scaling policies. HPA requires valid resource requests for utilization-based scaling and a working metrics pipeline. It cannot solve slow startup, external bottlenecks, or insufficient node capacity; combine it with readiness checks, load testing, sensible min/max replicas, and node autoscaling.
Cluster Autoscaler adjusts the number of worker nodes when Pods cannot schedule because of insufficient capacity and removes underutilized nodes when their Pods can be moved safely. It simulates scheduling against configured node groups rather than reacting directly to CPU percentage. Scale-down can be blocked by PodDisruptionBudgets, local storage, fixed node selectors, affinity, or non-evictable workloads. Correct requests are essential because the autoscaler reasons from scheduler demand. Define node-group limits, multiple zones, disruption-safe workloads, and monitoring for unschedulable Pods and failed scale-up events.
Difference between HPA and Cluster Autos: HPA scales application replicas, while Cluster Autoscaler scales worker nodes. HPA reacts to workload metrics and may create more Pods; if those Pods cannot fit, Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes based on their scheduling requirements. During falling load, HPA reduces replicas and Cluster Autoscaler may later remove empty or underutilized nodes. They solve different layers and normally work together. Both depend on accurate resource requests; poor requests can cause ineffective HPA targets, unschedulable Pods, wasted nodes, or unsafe consolidation.
A rolling update replaces old Pods gradually with new ones while keeping the application available. A Deployment controls the pace with `maxSurge` and `maxUnavailable`; readiness probes prevent unready replacements from receiving traffic. Kubernetes maintains old and new ReplicaSets and records rollout status, allowing `kubectl rollout status deployment/<name>` and `kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>`. Zero downtime also requires compatible database and API changes, graceful termination, sufficient capacity, and `progressDeadlineSeconds` so a stalled rollout is detected instead of hanging indefinitely.
The Recreate Deployment strategy terminates all old Pods before creating Pods for the new version. It is appropriate when two versions cannot run simultaneously, such as a workload using an exclusive resource or an application with incompatible concurrent state. It normally causes downtime between old-Pod termination and new-Pod readiness, so it is unsuitable for highly available request-serving systems unless another layer carries traffic. Database migrations, backups, rollback compatibility, maintenance communication, and readiness verification must be planned explicitly.
A Helm deployment installs or upgrades a versioned chart as a release. A safe command is `helm upgrade --install myapp ./chart -n production --create-namespace --values values-prod.yaml --atomic --wait --timeout 10m`. Templates render Kubernetes resources from chart defaults and supplied values; `helm lint` and `helm template` should run before deployment. Pin chart and image versions, keep secrets outside ordinary values files, validate generated manifests with policy checks, and inspect `helm status` and Kubernetes events when hooks or readiness cause a release to fail.
Helm rollback creates a new release revision using the manifests and values from an earlier revision. Inspect history with `helm history myapp -n production`, then run `helm rollback myapp <revision> -n production --wait --timeout 10m`. Rollback does not automatically reverse external side effects such as database migrations, deleted persistent data, or operator-managed resources. Charts therefore need backward-compatible schemas and explicitly reversible hooks. After rollback, verify Deployment rollout status, application health, error rate, and the exact image and configuration now serving traffic.
How do you troubleshoot ImagePullBackOff: Start with `kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <namespace>` and read the Events message; `ImagePullBackOff` is the retry delay after an image pull failure. Confirm the image name, tag or digest, registry, and whether the artifact exists. For `401` or `403`, verify `imagePullSecrets`, ServiceAccount association, workload identity, and registry permissions. For timeouts, test node DNS, routing, proxy, firewall, and registry availability. Also check node disk pressure and container-runtime logs. Correct the cause, then watch Events rather than repeatedly deleting the Pod.
How do you debug networking issues?: Trace one failing connection end to end. Confirm the Pod IP, readiness, and listening port with `kubectl get pod -o wide` and application logs; verify Service selectors and EndpointSlices with `kubectl get svc,endpointslice`. Test DNS using `nslookup` or `dig` from a diagnostic Pod, then test the Service and Pod IPs separately with `curl` or `nc`. Inspect NetworkPolicies, CNI status and logs, routes, node firewalls, kube-proxy or eBPF service state, and Ingress/Gateway events. Compare a working path and capture packets only after narrowing the failing hop.
